prompt.context: Our client is an organization that is trying to incentivize pharmaceutical and biotech firms to develop treatments and vaccines for diseases that are prevalent in developing countries. The challenge is to identify where to focus, as there are many possible diseases.
prompt.question: Which diseases represent the best opportunity for our client?

clarifying_info.a: DALY stands for disability-adjusted life year and is a measure of how much impact a disease has on people's productivity. Diseases that cause people to die young or that cause disability starting in childhood have the highest DALY scores.

clarifying_info.q: What does 'Pipeline' refer to on the exhibit?
clarifying_info.a: Pipeline indicates the number of drugs currently under development for that disease.
All these data are made up, as are some of the disease names.
Etiology means the causes of the disease.
Antigen is a general term that can refer to anything which provokes an immune response, whether bacteria, virus, etc.

clarifying_info.q: What does the Y-axis (Incidence) mean on the etiology chart?
clarifying_info.a: The Y-axis scale, incidence, indicates that 5% of cases are caused by Antigen A, and so forth. If someone adds up all the bars, they will realize they don't sum to 100% — this is because some cases are caused by antigens that have not yet been identified.

clarifying_info.q: How recent are the data and how large are the samples for the etiology chart?
clarifying_info.a: Data are from last year and sample sizes are large: n=1500 for the local population data and n=256 for the military data. Subjects in the local population data are children under 18. Subjects in the military data are soldiers of all ages.

exhibits.title: Disease in the Developing World
exhibits.shows: A scatter/bubble chart with Disease Burden (in DALYs, from Low to High) on the X-axis, number of existing treatments or vaccines (0–10) on the Y-axis, and bubble size representing the current drug pipeline. Multiple named diseases are plotted (including HIV, Hep, TB, Malaria, Diarrheal Disease, and others). Also on this page is a bar chart titled 'Etiology of Diarrheal Disease' showing the percentage of diarrheal disease cases caused by various antigens, with separate bars for local population (black) and military (white).
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0–10 existing treatments or vaccines. X-axis: Disease Burden in DALYs (Low to High). Bubble size = current pipeline. HIV and Hep appear at high disease burden with many existing treatments and large pipeline bubbles. TB, Malaria, and Diarrheal Disease appear at moderate-to-high disease burden with fewer existing treatments; Diarrheal Disease has the smallest pipeline bubble among this group. Etiology chart: multiple antigens shown; neither population's bars sum to 100% (some cases have unidentified causes).

exhibits.title: Prescribing Patterns in Market 1 vs. 2
exhibits.shows: A cumulative prescribing chart with physicians arranged in descending order of volume on the X-axis and cumulative percentage of total units prescribed on the Y-axis (0–100%). Two lines are shown: Market 1 (solid) and Market 2 (dashed).
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0–100% cumulative units. X-axis: physicians in descending order of volume. Market 1 line rises steeply — approximately the top one-third of physicians account for ~80% of units. Market 2 line rises more gradually — approximately the top 60% of physicians are needed to account for ~80% of units.

framework: Identify disease burden vs. current treatment/pipeline landscape to find underserved high-burden diseases
Analyze the specific disease chosen (diarrheal disease) in detail — etiology complexity, number of pathogens
Identify potential customer segments for a new treatment or vaccine
Assess risks and negotiating dynamics for each customer segment
Evaluate market entry strategy using prescribing concentration data to prioritize markets

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, which diseases represent the best opportunity for our client?
questions.guidance: HIV and Hep have the greatest disease burden but also many existing treatments and a large pipeline — hard to add incremental value. The next tier (TB, Malaria, Diarrheal Disease) has high burden with fewer existing treatments. Among these, Diarrheal Disease has the smallest pipeline, meaning there is the least competition and the most room for the client to incentivize new development. Recommend focusing on Diarrheal Disease.

questions.prompt: Given the client chose to focus on diarrheal disease, what does Exhibit 1's etiology chart tell us about it?
questions.guidance: Diarrheal disease is not caused by a single primary antigen — it can be caused by a large number of different pathogens. This makes developing a treatment or vaccine difficult because it cannot simply target one antigen; it needs to be effective across many. This is analogous to the flu or the common cold. This pattern holds for both the local population and the military population. The fact that bars do not sum to 100% means some causative agents remain unidentified, making the problem even harder.

questions.prompt: Who would be the main customers if a treatment or vaccine for diarrheal disease were produced?
questions.guidance: Strong answers should surface at least: (1) Governments of countries where diarrheal disease is prevalent — large-volume buyers; (2) Nonprofits providing healthcare in developing regions; (3) International organizations such as WHO/UN. Interviewer should keep probing until candidate also identifies: (4) Foreign tourists traveling to affected regions; (5) The military (e.g., US soldiers deployed in endemic areas) — both represent significant additional revenue streams.

questions.prompt: What are the issues or risks the drug maker would face with each of these customers?
questions.guidance: Governments and the military are attractive because they buy in large volumes, but that same concentration gives them significant negotiating power. If the military declines to purchase, that single lost sale could make the entire project unprofitable. The client and drug maker should consider setting up pre-commitment contracts with governments and the military to reduce this risk. Tourists are a more fragmented customer base with less negotiating power but also lower volume certainty.

questions.prompt: Examine Exhibit 2. What does it show, and which market seems like a better initial target?
questions.guidance: The chart shows physicians in each market arranged by prescribing volume in descending order; the Y-axis tracks cumulative percentage of total units prescribed. Market 1 is more concentrated: roughly the top one-third of physicians account for ~80% of units. Market 2 is less concentrated: roughly the top 60% of physicians are needed to reach ~80% of units. Because Market 1 is more concentrated, fewer physicians need to be informed and convinced to prescribe a new comparable product — sales force effort is lower, market penetration is easier, and it is a better initial target.

math.setup: Approximate read-off from the cumulative prescribing curve. For Market 1: x% of physicians (sorted descending) → 80% of cumulative units. For Market 2: y% of physicians → 80% of cumulative units.
steps: Market 1: ~33% of physicians account for ~80% of units
Market 2: ~60% of physicians needed to account for ~80% of units
Implication: Market 1 requires targeting ~27 percentage points fewer physicians to achieve equivalent coverage
math.answer: Market 1 is more concentrated and is the better initial target for launch.

brainstorming.prompt: Who would be the main customers for a diarrheal disease treatment or vaccine, and what are the key risks for each?

categories.name: Government buyers
ideas: Ministries of health in developing countries with high prevalence
Large-volume purchases but high negotiating power
Risk: single government refusing purchase can sink profitability

categories.name: Non-governmental organizations / nonprofits
ideas: Health-focused NGOs operating in endemic areas
May act as distribution channel as well as buyer

categories.name: Military
ideas: Armed forces deployed to endemic regions (e.g., US soldiers in Egypt)
Concentrated buyer with large volume — significant negotiating power
Risk: if military declines, project may become unprofitable

categories.name: Travelers / tourists
ideas: More fragmented buyer base, lower negotiating power
Sold via travel clinics and pharmacies
More predictable demand tied to travel volumes

recommendation: Focus on diarrheal disease, which has high burden in developing countries, few existing treatments, and the thinnest current pipeline — representing the clearest gap the client can help fill
Pursue development of a broad-spectrum treatment/vaccine given the multi-antigen etiology of diarrheal disease
Target Market 1 for initial launch given its higher physician prescribing concentration, enabling efficient sales force deployment
risks: Multi-pathogen etiology makes development technically challenging and costly
Large government and military customers hold significant negotiating power and concentration risk
Unidentified antigens mean the treatment may not be fully effective across all cases
Pre-commitment contracts may be difficult to negotiate, leaving demand uncertain
next_steps: Negotiate pre-commitment purchase agreements with target governments and military buyers before committing to full R&D investment
Conduct deeper market sizing for the tourist and military segments to quantify incremental revenue potential
Assess feasibility of a broad-spectrum formulation vs. targeting the highest-incidence antigens first
Develop a go-to-market plan focusing sales efforts on the top-third of prescribing physicians in Market 1
